outlier.evidence: Ratings 5, 6, 6, 7 lie within one point of the mean 6.0. The one rating below threshold, Reviewer_kMiC's 5, is principled: its points on the exponential dependence on r and d, the '≈' in Theorem 4.3 and the undiscussed 1/alpha^4 rate are all in the submission.

Checklist item 3 is N/A throughout; l.370-371 name an empirical study as future work.

checkable_claims.claim: The optimization uses no sparsity-encouraging or low-rank prior, so a polynomial rather than logarithmic sample complexity is expected.
checkable_claims.evidence: Table 1 and (11): the constraint set Lambda is an l1,1 ball, a nuclear-norm ball, or both. What holds is that Theorem 4.3 gains nothing from them: the bound is polynomial in k1k2 for every choice of norm.

rebuttal.evidence: Reviewer_sAxR edited the review on 2021-08-19 and wrote that day: 'I increased my score to 6.' Reviewer_kMiC's edit (2021-07-22) predates the author response (2021-08-10), and kMiC never replied. Reviewer_SSuU replied on 2021-08-31 ('Thanks a lot for clarifying all my questions!') and kept 7 with no edit. Reviewer_kDGo did not reply.
rebuttal.what_convinced_or_not: sAxR still wanted experiments but judged the finite-sample and computational results 'good enough to make up for the lack of an experimental study', citing the other reviewers. kMiC's points were largely conceded (a matrix formulation suffices; r and d must be O(log k1k2); '≈' to be removed) and drew no reply. SSuU's sharper question, whether the hardness results [23, 48] survive Assumption 4.1, got an argument by example (sparse Ising models), not a proof.

ac.evidence: 'This paper was viewed as a borderline paper'; acceptance matches three of four ratings at or above 6. The AC echoes Reviewer_kMiC on tensor notation and Reviewer_sAxR and Reviewer_kDGo on experiments, then argues for acceptance from its own reading: 'a new idea that can inspire other researchers' on 'such a fundamental problem as finding alternatives to MLE'. It adds a doubt about sparse models that no A reviewer raised, on a wrong premise (see checkable claims).

A tractable alternative to the MLE for a fundamental problem, with consistency, asymptotic normality and polynomial finite-sample bounds.
The AC's own judgement that the loss is 'a new idea that can inspire other researchers'.
The rate, the constants r and d, the tensor notation and the missing experiments treated as revisions; Reviewer_sAxR rose to 6, accepting theory in place of experiments.

checkable_claims.evidence: The second half holds: Theorem 4.3 charges max(k1k2n, c(Lambda)) per iteration, and Definition 2.1 centers Phi by E_U[Phi(x)], an integral over X whose cost is never stated. checkable_claims.evidence: True of the paper as written, which assumes exact centering. The obstacle is weaker than stated: X is a box or a ball in every example, so uniform Monte Carlo approximates E_U[Phi] for any bounded Phi; what is missing is an analysis of that error. The camera-ready (Section 5, 'Practicality of Algorithm 1') concedes that centering 'may not be polynomial-time'.

verdict: Both committees recommended a poster for the same reasons, on matching score profiles: A 5, 6, 6, 7 (mean 6.0) and B 7, 7, 6, 5 (mean 6.25). Each saw a clean theory result on a basic problem (a convex loss that avoids the partition function, with consistency, asymptotic normality and polynomial finite-sample bounds) and treated its weaknesses as revisions. In each committee one reviewer rose to 6 after the rebuttal (Reviewer_sAxR, Reviewer_xSou) and one 5 stayed (Reviewer_kMiC, Reviewer_nf2S). The committees found different weaknesses, and the submission confirms most of them. A pressed the statistics: (k1k2)^2/alpha^4 samples (Theorem 4.3), exp(r^T d) in the step size and iteration count (Lemma 3.1), and '≈' inside theorems. B pressed computation and prior art: the gradient needs a centering integral that the paper never costs (Definition 2.1; Theorem 4.3 charges k1k2n per gradient), and the loss extends Vuffray et al.'s uncited 2016 interaction screening objective. Neither committee treated any of this as fatal, and nobody argued for more than a poster: the top ratings are 7s, A's 7 wrongly credits the paper with asymptotic efficiency, and B's two 7s rest on a two-sentence review and a 2-hour review. The ACs differ only in emphasis. A's AC accepted a 'borderline paper' on its own reading ('a new idea that can inspire other researchers'); B's AC deferred to the reviewers and made the gradient-cost caveat a condition of the final version.
